speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Okay, I will not take a short break and adjournment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will still have the Second Reading of the Computer Misuse (Amendment) Bill to comply with the procedural requirements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scammers lurk in every corner and victims are often caught unawares.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In Singapore, the number of scams has also increased sharply.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is more than a fivefold increase since 2018.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scam cases are now more than one-and-a-half times that of physical crime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Back in 2018, they were only a quarter.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amount of money lost to scams is staggering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many of us know or have personally heard stories of people who have fallen prey.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They include elderly Singaporeans who lost their life savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, more than half of scam victims in 2022 were aged 20 to 39.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Victims often lose more than money – they lose peace of mind, sense of well-being, relations with family sometimes become very strained and all of these things bring about great distress.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many scams in Singapore have an overseas nexus.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We cannot stop the global tide but must do everything we can to try and keep the scammers far from shore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bills we are debating today are part of the Government's multi-pronged strategy to fight scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have been educating the public so that they are aware of the signs of scam and know what actions they can take to protect themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members would have seen the public campaign, "I can ACT against Scams", or hosted outreach sessions by Police officers in their constituency events involving residents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have taken proactive measures to prevent scammers from being able to reach victims in the first place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has been working with the telcos to block spoofed calls from reaching Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier this Sitting, we tabled the Online Criminal Harms Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Among other things, the Online Criminal Harms Bill will help to stop potential scams from taking place, or as soon as they are detected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also made it easier to detect and report scams and follow-up with partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police set up the Anti-Scam Command in 2022 to consolidate expertise and resources in combatting scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Staff from the major banks are co-located with the Police, so that all the parties can quickly act together to freeze scam-tainted accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the help of our foreign partners, Police brought down 13 scam syndicates in 2022.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More than 70 persons based overseas were arrested.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bills we are proposing today will add to our suite of anti-scam measures outlined above.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We propose to empower the authorities to deal more effectively with money mules and to prevent the abuse of Singpass for scam operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, let me explain the role of money mules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are individuals who allow criminals to control their bank or other payment accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They also include those who use their accounts to receive or transfer monies under the criminals' instructions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members may recall the OCBC phishing scam that occurred between December 2021 and January 2022 – 790 victims fell prey.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this scam, the Police identified more than 120 suspected money mules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More than 120 local bank accounts were used to receive the scam victims' monies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scam syndicates typically cultivate a network of money mules to facilitate their crimes or to launder criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The money mules' bank accounts form a web of multiple accounts; scammed monies can be split into different denominations and transferred through these accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This process is repeated many times over, so that the monies go through multiple layers of bank accounts, before being transferred out of Singapore into the hands of the syndicate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This tactic of "layering" is designed to make it difficult for the authorities to follow the money trail and to get to the perpetrators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Between 2020 and 2022, scammers exploited more than 38,000 bank accounts to launder their proceeds from local victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over the same period, more than 19,000 money mules were investigated by the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One big problem for the Police is that with electronic transactions, all these actions that I described earlier happen very quickly, often in a matter of hours.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another problem is that when interviewed by the Police, most of the money mules claimed they did not know that they were handling illegal funds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They claimed not to have known the identity of the person who instructed them, nor the identity of the bank account holders whom they were receiving funds from or transferring funds to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many agreed to facilitate these money transfers because they were paid to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They claimed that they did not think that they were doing anything illegal and did not know they were dealing with criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The fact is, however, that their actions caused great harm to scam victims, whose monies have been moved beyond reach, beyond our ability to recover.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides money mules, the Police have also observed a trend of scam syndicates abusing Singpass to facilitate their criminal activities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, syndicates recruit Singpass users with the promise of monetary gain and then use the Singpass accounts to further their schemes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scam syndicates who get hold of another person's Singpass credentials can use them to open bank accounts, which are then used to receive and transfer funds obtained through scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Irresponsible Singpass users have facilitated this by selling or sharing their Singpass credentials, such as their Singpass password and SMS one-time password.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Scam syndicates effectively assume the identity of a Singpass user for their criminal activities and exploit the Singpass account to commit criminal activities while hiding their own tracks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a result, these scam syndicates are extremely difficult to pursue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This includes recognising the limitations of current laws, which make it difficult to take the money mules to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It requires the Prosecution to prove that the money mule had knowledge or reasonable grounds to believe that the monies transacted through his bank account are linked to criminal activity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Out of 19,000, fewer than 250 ended up being prosecuted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Think about that, it is fewer than one in 10.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, it has been challenging to prove the wrongful intention of those who give up their Singpass credentials under existing laws like the Computer Misuse Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clearly, there is a gap that has allowed money mules to continue abetting scammers at little cost to themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Why should they be deterred if they can evade prosecution by simply claiming ignorance?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The two sets of amendments we are proposing are, therefore, intended to strengthen our collective defence against scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, it sets guardrails on the use of bank and Singpass accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Bank account holders and Singpass users must be careful and exercise diligence regarding their bank accounts and Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our bank accounts and Singpass accounts are for our own use.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should not allow them to be used by another person, especially if we do not know who the other party is or what the transactions are for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, the amendments will empower the Police to act more effectively against those who blatantly ignore these guardrails, and abuse or allow to be abused, their bank accounts and Singpass credentials to perpetrate scams and other crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will first explain the proposed amendments to the CDSA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are defined in sections 26(E) and 26(F) of the existing Penal Code and are also applied in the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A person can be liable for rash money laundering if he proceeded to carry out a transaction while he had some suspicions about the transaction, but did not make further enquiries to address those suspicions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A person can be liable for negligent money laundering if he continued with a transaction despite the presence of red flags or suspicious indicators, which would be noticeable by an ordinary, reasonable person.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These changes will allow a money laundering offence to be made out against an individual at a lower level of culpability, compared with the current laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Which of these offences are made out, if any, will depend on the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Person A responds to an online job advertisement seeking to hire an accounts manager.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A was told that he would be paid $2,000 a month to receive money using his personal bank account and all he had to do was to transfer sums of more than $100,000 to other bank accounts weekly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is all the job requires, allowing the bank account to be used for transfer of monies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is nothing like the kind of work that would justify a monthly salary of $2,000 that we would normally expect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Despite the exceptional attractiveness of this job, which should have raised suspicions, A did not verify the source of the funds he was receiving, the purpose of the transfers nor the authenticity of his purported employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Due to the frequency and amount of money transacted, A suspected that the monies could be criminal proceeds, but he chose to carry on without further checks and the money was eventually found to be criminal proceeds from scam victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will also share an example of negligent money laundering.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Person B responded to an online advertisement on a social media platform calling for people to "rent out" their bank accounts; it literally used those terms – "rent out".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: B provided the Internet banking login details for his personal bank account to an unknown subject and was paid $800 to let his personal bank account be used by that subject.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: B did not know what his bank account was used for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: B claimed that he did not suspect anything wrong with the arrangement despite receiving this quite easy $800.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Investigations found that his bank account was used to receive about $20,000 from a Singaporean victim of a love scam.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To an ordinary reasonable person, this offer would have sounded suspicious and really "too good to be true".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A money mule can be held liable for this offence if his conduct falls within any of the following four circumstances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One, the value of the property he dealt with is disproportionate to his known sources of income; or two, he allowed another person, or persons, to access, operate or control his payment account and failed to take reasonable steps to find out the purpose of this arrangement; or three, he received or transferred money using his payment account and failed to take reasonable steps to find out the source or destination of the money; or four, he received money from or transferred money to another person or persons and failed to take reasonable steps to find out that person's identity and physical location.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will cite an example to illustrate the above offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Person C responded to a job advertisement by a company.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: C is told he will earn $100 a day for using his own bank account to receive money from the company's customers and transfer the money to the company's bank account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All these from a purported employer whom he does not ever meet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As unusual as the job may have sounded, C did not question why he needed to use his personal account to receive and transfer money from the company's customers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He did not take steps to find out where the money was coming from or going to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After all, the effort required of him is quite minimal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While clause 7 provides that a person could be liable for an offence under any of the four circumstances I described earlier, clause 7 also provides in the new subsection 55A that it is a defence if the person is able to prove that he did not know and had no reason to believe that the property he had dealt with directly through his account, or indirectly, was criminal proceeds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I mentioned the worrying trend of Singpass users who give away their Singpass credentials, often for money.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The actions of such errant Singpass users facilitate scams and other criminal conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They undermine Singpass as our national digital identity service which many people have come to depend on for digital transactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it is challenging to take such errant Singpass users to task.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, under the CMA today, it must be proven that the Singpass user knowingly disclosed his credentials for wrongful gain or an unlawful purpose, or that it would cause wrongful loss, which is difficult to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In one recent case, one Singpass user who had sold his login credentials subsequently pretended to be a victim and came to the Police, claiming that he had been deceived into giving up his Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was only through extensive investigations, taking up enormous Police resources, that the Singpass user eventually admitted to have sold his credentials, knowing that his Singpass would be used for criminal activities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in many others, the Singpass users are uncooperative in investigations and fabricate stories about how their Singpass came to be abused.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are concerned with the behaviour of Singpass users who disclose their Singpass passwords or access codes, or who provide any means of accessing their Singpass accounts in situations where the credentials can then be used to facilitate criminal conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In my speech, for ease of reference, I will refer to all of these types of acts collectively as "disclosing Singpass credentials".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To combat such behaviour, it will now be an offence for a Singpass user to disclose his Singpass credentials, if he did so knowing, or having reasonable grounds to believe, that the purpose of the disclosure is for any person to commit, or facilitate the commission by any person, of any offence under any written law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The intent of this change is not to make legitimate users of Singpass fearful of disclosing their credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They should, however, be aware that in certain situations, the disclosure could be an offence if, one, the disclosure was carried out for any form of gain; two, the disclosure was carried out with the knowledge it would likely cause wrongful loss to any person; or three, the disclosure was carried out but without reasonable steps being taken to find out the identity and physical location of the person to whom the credentials were disclosed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These proposed provisions are based on actual situations Police have observed, where individuals have deliberately sold or disclosed their Singpass credentials to criminal syndicates.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Again, to be abundantly clear, it is not our intent to criminalise situations where there is a genuine need to share credentials for legitimate transactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, seniors may, in some situations, need the help of their family members to make Singpass transactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new provisions are also not intended to capture persons who were genuinely tricked into giving up their Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to deal with those who purchase Singpass credentials and syndicates which trade the Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bill introduces provisions in section 8B to clarify the scope of this new offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not an offence if an individual obtained or retained another person's Singpass credentials for a legitimate purpose.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is also not an offence if an individual supplied, offered to supply, transmitted or made available the Singpass credentials of another person for a legitimate purpose and the individual did not know or have reason to believe that those credentials will be or are likely to be used to commit an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The nature of scam syndicates is that they operate mostly from overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regardless of where these offences are committed, it is critical for us to prevent conduct that amounts to an abuse of Singpass to facilitate scams and other criminal activities and to protect Singpass as Singapore's national digital identity service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They seek to disrupt the operations of criminals preying on Singaporeans by acting as guardrails for the use of payment accounts and Singpass credentials and allowing Police to better act against money mules and those who abuse Singpass to perpetrate scams and other crimes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the increase in instances of reported cases of scams both globally and in Singapore, our fellow Singaporeans are even more susceptible to risks of being scammed and taken advantage of as unwitting money mules.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have heard from the Minister just now on the facts and figures.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we can increase public vigilance and awareness in our defence against scams, we need our legislative framework to remain up to date with technological developments in order to disrupt the operations of scammers, which are increasingly more sophisticated and challenging.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One aspect is the use of money mules as a means to facilitate scams and getting scam proceeds out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is almost 20% of the entire scams in terms of quantum.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Money mules are a key part of scammers' operations here in Singapore and I agree that there is a lacuna in the law that needs to be plugged.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, the evidential challenge is to prove that money mules have actual knowledge or intent to facilitate such criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, money mules are currently charged under the Computer Misuse Act for abetting a person to gain access to the bank account without authority.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This provision does not seem the most appropriate for the acts committed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I welcome the changes proposed by the Bill and their direct intervention in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My firm is part of the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) acting for accused persons on a pro bono basis and we see some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: From experience, not all alleged money mules fit the typical stereotype of a criminal scammer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of them claim or maybe are as much victims of circumstances as the scammed victims themselves.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If I may share a case about one such young accused person that walked through our office doors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He saw a job advertisement and responded to it with the intention of working to support his family of seven and supplement the income of the sole breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He ended up giving up control of his bank account and Singpass to an unknown person in return for payment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He thought this is his income or salary.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But it was too good to be true.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He faces charges now, accused of being a money mule.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides that case, I have also received appeals during my Meet-the-People Sessions from families in Keat Hong who also faced similar situations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mostly, these money mules were lured by the prospect of job opportunities and some were scammed out of their savings and forced to act as money mules in order to regain some of those monies back.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that the amendments strike a balance between protecting the public and also meting out the appropriate penalties commensurate to the crime and culpability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments to the law will place the burden on the accused money mule to prove that he or she had reasonable grounds to believe that the disclosure of his or her Singpass was lawful and to take reasonable steps to ascertain the purpose of the person accessing the account and the source of funds and/or the person's identity in relation to the bank account.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In practice, it is likely that the person will face difficulty to prove otherwise and may be found guilty under the amended provisions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is despite the fact that he or she may not have had any knowledge as to how the bank account was being used.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are various offences, such as rash or negligent money laundering, where the accused money mule has a suspicion that the monies could be criminal proceeds but chose not to verify the legitimacy of such funds.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If I may ask, what would be the reasonable steps that a person can take to make such verifications?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry can consider forming a public reporting office which provides an avenue through the anti-scam hotline or an enhancement on the ScamShield app for members of the public and those who genuinely intend to make such verifications.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This way, a person can just make a call, alert the agencies or banks of such offer or make verifications for such transactions before it is being made.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This can come under the suspicious transactions reporting office for AML transactions, something which our ordinary members of the public may not be aware of.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, the burden of proof is about to shift, some say, in a drastic manner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I wonder if the Ministry may wish to consider delaying the implementation of the amendments while carrying out public education events as to the seriousness of such offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because the advertisements are framed as job advertisements, many young persons or even older ones may not appreciate that.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just by letting another person access their Singpass or bank account, they are committing a serious offence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Or as the Minister mentioned, the disclosing of their Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, such awareness campaigns should be done in concert with the banks and financial institutions, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and potential employers as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The risk and dangers of being used as money mules can be amplified through our job seeking portals to alert potential jobseekers of the scams and pitfalls out there.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, I agree with the amendments under the Computer Misuse Act to protect the use of our Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to have a more robust way of protecting the vulnerable groups of our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps, the use of data analytics to see the pattern of access by such groups can also help alert or red flag any sudden unathorised access.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, when I do my house visits and my AICs, the volunteers are quite aware in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This does not just affect the elderly but also the young who are looking for jobs and to earn a decent and honest living, and maybe may not have had the full brunt of life experiences before them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our people's hard-earned money and lifesavings are at risk and at stake and, with that, their hopes and aspirations for a better future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not only have these victims lost significant amounts of hard-earned monies or retirement savings, they also lived with the mental anguish and guilt of being gullible enough to fall for such deception.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Often, the victims were vulnerable in certain ways and susceptible to exploitation, such as those who live alone and are desperate for friends to chat with, or those searching for a life partner, who then become the victim of a love scam.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some may blame the victims for being foolish or authors of their own misfortune.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But this ignores the fact that we are dealing here with perpetrators who are parts of organised syndicates who appear well-trained to find targets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After their ordeals, victims usually report the matter to the Police, hoping that their monies can be recovered or, at the very least, that the perpetrators would be arrested, prosecuted and punished.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Due to the organised nature of scams, which are often transnational, Police have the unenviable task of informing victims that their chances of recovering their monies are often slim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such news to a younger victim is certainly bad news, but at least he or she has the potential to recover from the loss.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such news to a retiree, however, can be crushing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Scams have become a major crime issue in Singapore, warranting the Police to issue separate scam updates in their annual crime reporting since last year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These Bills tighten the net around those who facilitate money laundering, including letting their bank accounts and Singpass accounts be used for fund transfers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Reducing the opportunities for syndicates to redirect the fruits of crime is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to how effective these provisions will be to disrupt the operations of criminal syndicates, only time will tell.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have three clarifications and concerns about the CDSA (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, on the difficulties of prosecuting money mules currently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could MHA clarify whether the balance 98.7% of cases were all not prosecuted due to the difficulties in proving intention or does this number include non-prosecutions due to other grounds as well?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The punishment for such acts of rashness or negligence will be lower than for acts done deliberately or with knowledge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the earlier statistic of not being able to prosecute more than 98% of money mules investigated in the last three years, what is MHA's assessment of how these changes will improve prosecution rates in future?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is stated in the explanatory statement to the Bill that the new section 55A is meant to criminalise certain acts that facilitate money laundering "regardless of a person's mental state".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My concern here is about persons who may be manipulated into letting others use their bank accounts to transfer money.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I encountered one resident recently who told me that her bank account had been frozen by Police as it had apparently been used to make or receive some suspicious funds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I tried asking her how her account got compromised, but she was unable to answer coherently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the law then, a suspected money mule is expected to make some sort of reasoned assessment about the nature of the transaction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the authorities approach a case where the suspect appears to be mentally impaired?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The current situation is very concerning on several counts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe I am watching too many Mediacorp programmes, but are we seeing the return of triads, only this time, triads in digital skin?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, with the amendments to the CDSA and CMA Bills, it will give the appropriate power to the authorities to take action and I hope will also deter persons who think this is easy money to recognise the severity of their actions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we do not want Singaporeans to lose confidence in moving to digital.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Digital is here to stay and, in fact, will accelerate and become more pervasive in our lives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, it becomes even more important for Singaporeans to be digital first, even if not digital only.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has assured us in previous speeches that, for Singapore, we are definitely going to take care of those who are less digitally savvy but it does not mean that we are going to go back to the old ages of totally non-digital just because we have such situations going on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, I do have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (b) There has been a lot of efforts in driving awareness of importance and responsibility of protecting one's digital identity and digital footprint across the board, from banking access to social media and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What else is the Government planning to do to increase the effectiveness of these initiatives and what else needs to be done by the banks, financial services institutions, the community and the rest of Government?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is probably no longer secure enough to use a login with simply a password and a one-time password (OTP).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All this, of course, leads to more costs being involved and more steps.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But it looks to me that this may be required.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, how is the Government planning to fight this kind of crime?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In lieu of COSMIC going online, what data will the Government use to strengthen enforcement of this Bill?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (e) Enforcement of Computer Misuse legislation can be challenging due to several factors, including the rapidly evolving technology.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, how is Singapore planning to keep pace with new forms of cybercrime and methods of committing offences and enable MHA to be able to identify and prosecute perpetrators and the syndicates involved?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: (f) With the Internet enabling global communication and transactions as we have seen in past cases, cybercrimes often occur across multiple jurisdictions, making it challenging to identify and prosecute offenders.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The victims need to be protected as much as possible and, where possible, the victims are supported as much as possible with recovering the monies that have been scammed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What else beyond the initiatives already in place will the Government be planning to put into action that can help the victims recover as much of the monies that have been scammed?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And perhaps a little bit of compassion from the banks would help, because, in fact, in 2021, a very good friend of mine had somebody, her friend who was totally scammed and then the bank locked down all her bank accounts and she was left borrowing money from other friends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, certainly, we hope that we need to have a little bit of compassion for the victims and ensure that there is a systematic approach to helping them and supporting them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But, of course, the most important help is to tell them not to give away their identity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, in conclusion, to overcome these challenges, MHA and Anti-Scam Centre Singapore as well as CSA need to work closely with technology experts, cybersecurity professionals and other stakeholders like the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the banks as well as international communities to stay abreast of emerging threats and develop effective strategies for preventing and prosecuting computer misuse crimes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will involve investing in new technology, enhancing international cooperation and improving training and resources for all personnel involved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, Mr Deputy Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the new offences of rash and negligent money laundering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A person may commit an offence if they enter into an arrangement acting rashly as to the fact that it relates to benefits from criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry for Home Affairs (MHA) has said that a person acts rashly if they had suspicions but did not make further enquiries to address those suspicions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the offence require that the person must be suspicious that the arrangement is linked to criminal conduct?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is it sufficient that the person is suspicious that the facts they were given, for example, people's identities or reasons for the transaction that may not be true?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the extent of verification that a person should make to address any suspicions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A person may also commit an offence if they negligently enter into such an arrangement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MHA explained that a person is negligent if they continue with a transaction despite the presence of "red flags" that are noticeable by an ordinary, reasonable person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate further on what these "red flags" are?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Money mules who are implicated in money laundering may not have a clear understanding of money laundering arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, they may be elderly persons or less financially sophisticated persons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain if the standards of the "ordinary, reasonable person" will be calibrated to factor in the individual characteristics of the accused?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the new offences under both Bills which involve a failure to verify details.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, can the Minister elaborate on the extent of verification that is expected?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is possible that an individual may provide another with access to their account or to their Singpass credentials for a legitimate purpose, but the access is later abused for criminal purposes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what is expected of the individual in this situation to avoid committing an offence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there an ongoing requirement that the individual periodically verifies the transactions going through their account?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, an elderly parent may give their children access to their account to help manage their finances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They may also give their children their Singpass details to help with a transaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While MHA has stated that owners of payment accounts must be responsible for how their accounts are being used, the reality is that a financially illiterate elderly person may trust their children and be content to leave control of their accounts to their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also possible that they may not be in a position to regain control of their accounts after allowing their children initial access, even if they are aware that the accounts are being used for illegitimate purposes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how the Police will view such cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the responsibility of network access facility operators and service providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Computer Misuse Bill clarifies that network access facility operators and service providers are not guilty of making available any Singpass information that comes across their platforms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, platforms, too, have a role to play in addressing illegal or harmful content transmitted on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what it views as the responsibility of network access facility operators and service providers in addressing the illegal use of accounts and Singpass credentials?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the regulatory frameworks in place to ensure that network access facility operators and service providers are not complicit in the use of their platforms for illegal purposes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Madam, I stand in support of the Bills.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These Bills are really about equipping our Home Team with the necessary legal tools to combat the scourge of scams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Second Minister for Home Affairs apprised us of the staggering numbers involved here – tens of thousands of victims, tens of thousands of bank accounts used to launder money from local victims, and billions of dollars lost.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The pain and suffering caused to the victims of the scams is very real.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have spoken to several residents in the Bukit Batok Single Member Constituency who have fallen victim to scams and lost their life savings to criminals who preyed on their vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is heartbreaking for them to realise that, given the international nature of these crimes, there is little prospect of them recovering their monies stolen from them once the monies get transferred overseas, despite the best efforts of our enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The introduction of these Bills represents a decisive step in Home Team's strategy to deal with this scourge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our officers from the Anti-Scam Command (ASC), which includes the Scam Strike Teams in all land divisions, have been working feverishly on thousands of cases since the Command was set up last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Frequently, cross-border cooperation is needed to bring perpetrators to book and recover funds transmitted overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, speed is of the essence as these officers, through their network of more than 80 partners, try to freeze and recover monies belonging to the victims before they leave our jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These officers deserve our appreciation and full support as they discharge their duties to the best of their abilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have no issue with the proposal to extend criminal liability to an account holder who engaged in rash money laundering activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I see it, the account holder would have been put on notice but decided to assume the risk nonetheless, usually for profit, as explained by the hon Second Minister in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The reality is that account holders have different levels of knowledge and experiences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Their susceptibility to overtures and influences of a scammer may also vary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is an observation made by the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim in her speech yesterday and by the hon Member Mr Louis Ng in his speech today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these circumstances, to apply an objective standard may operate unfairly against some of the account holders who do not have sufficient knowledge and experience and, therefore, are less discerning than others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, I do appreciate though that this may give a free pass to too many people who can feign ignorance after the fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially unhelpful, given the sheer number of scams that we face on a daily basis – on an industrial scale, actually.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Clearly, there is a pressing need to clamp down on accounts that may be accessible by scammers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I appreciate why a tough stance has to be taken.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder though, if the potential harsh effect of applying an objective standard on certain account holders, by reason of their personal backgrounds, can be mitigated by two measures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By lodging the Police report, the ASC will be placed in a position to freeze the monies in the accounts and prevent the monies from falling into hands of the scammers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the account holders who do not act with diligence, I will imagine that the penny would drop for them as soon as they are put into funds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, these account holders should be incentivised and given credit for proactively reaching out to the authorities in such circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that the hon Second Minister mentioned that the rash or negligence concept is not new and is employed in the Penal Code as well as the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would suggest that the hon Minister consider the approach taken under the Immigration Act in relation to persons who are found to have harboured immigration offenders as a result of their negligence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As some Members here may recall, in the 1980s, we had a big problem with illegal immigrants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the Government passed strict laws to deal with this problem by making it an offence for employers and landlords to harbour illegal immigrants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1993 and later in 1998, the Government set out the due diligence requirements in legislation, so that employers and landlords were put on notice on the checks they have to perform, failing which they will be deemed not to have exercised due diligence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In short, all these measures will make it harder for someone to say, "But I didn't know!".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The response would be, "Well, you ought to have known." I also would like to take this opportunity, as an aside, to deal with a scenario that I believe may come up from time to time in Police investigations against suspected money mules for not exercising due diligence in allowing their accounts to be used by others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The suspects may explain that this is because the subject to whom he provided access to his account is unbanked, meaning that they had no access to a banking account, and had sought his assistance to receive or send monies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst at first glance this explanation may be rejected as being unbelievable, there is anecdotal and statistical evidence to suggest otherwise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have also come across cases of adult Singaporeans who have not being able to open bank accounts because of their criminal past, or because they are subject to investigations of certain offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This should be a universal right and, in fact, this is not a controversial point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that in 2020, Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, in response to a Parliamentary Question filed by the hon Member Louis Chua, stated that MAS was working with banks on further ways to enhance financial inclusion whilst ensuring that risks were adequately managed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should we be able to ensure that all Singaporean residents have universal access to banking services, this can help in the fight against scams too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Money mules will no longer be able to provide the excuse that the third party who took control of their account is unbanked.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now proceed to deal with the proposed amendments to the CMA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the hon Second Minister's proposal to make it an offence for an individual to disclose his Singpass credentials to another knowingly or having reasonable grounds to believe that the purpose of the disclosure is to facilitate the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such access would enable criminals to open bank accounts, registering companies and sign up for new phone lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is one further area that I would like to respectfully suggest to the hon Second Minister with a view to further bolster the steps, to prevent unauthorised disclosure of Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As part of our efforts to be a digital nation, the Government offers Singpass Application Programming Interface (API) to both Government and private entities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, Singaporeans now, through Singpass, can gain access to a plethora of services provided by both Government and private entities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the convenience, unfortunately, comes the risk of some Singaporeans being scammed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have heard and seen cases of people falling prey to phishing and spoofing scams by scammers allegedly representing the Government and private entities that led them to disclose their Singpass credentials to scammers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this reason, I would like to suggest that it should be made a regulatory must for all entities using Singpass APIs for access into their services be given the responsibility to proactively conduct due diligence to identify phishing and spoofing attempts on unsuspecting people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By imposing a regulatory responsibility, I hope that alarm can be raised sooner rather than later and the number of victims falling prey to such scams can be reduced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no sure way to guard against the ill intentions of malicious men, just as there is no way to match the ingenuity of criminal minds, save by the ingenuity of all of us who stand against them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My first set of proposals requires the presence of minds from individuals to pay attention to the rules of engagement in a digital world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My second requires institutions to play this role too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Together, we can form a tighter net against those would wish us harm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Correspondingly, this comes with the increasing prevalence of digital transactions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a financial hub, it is imperative that we tighten our legislations on the digital front.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments to the two Bills are therefore timely and necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I wish to raise some general queries on the implementation of the two Bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recent media reports have shed light on a different aspect of scamming incidents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, some individuals who were believed to be scammers, were, in fact, victims of scam syndicates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may have been lured into committing offences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From such incidents, we understand that there is a myriad of factors involved.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes the fact that these individuals may themselves have been deceived and were unaware as to where the truth lies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the constantly evolving nature and increasing complexity of scams, how does the Ministry ascertain whether a suspect is adequately educated, or can recognise a scam?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry determine whether the suspect was cognisant of their role in a scam?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, how will the changes proposed in the Bills specifically address the challenges?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My second concern is regarding the enforcement of penalties against criminal masterminds in scam and cybercrime syndicates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While going after the small fry or runners is important to break the chain, these people are just a cog in the wheel, who are easily replaceable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to also target the mastermind behind these criminal operations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government share what is being done to track the syndicate masterminds, even if the crimes are transnational in nature?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it may not be directly under the purview of the two Bills, can the Government share what is being done to track and retrieve the amount of money stolen via cybercrimes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the current success rate of the retrieval of stolen funds?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an issue that is of utmost importance to scam victims and residents who are becoming increasingly wary of cyber transactions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, while we take action against those who intentionally give away their Singpass credentials for criminal activities, we must also consider the security weaknesses that may lead to the compromise of Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These deficiencies can arise from both technological vulnerabilities and social engineering, such as manipulating not just the user, but also customer service staff who handle the affected accounts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are Government taking to enhance the security of these systems?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we leverage technology to prevent users from unintentionally or wilfully disclosing their Singpass login information during any part of the login process?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the system require additional levels of authentication to ensure better safeguards?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government balance the need for increased authentication, with the goal of expanding the use of Singpass for various transactions and services, which is a critical aspect of our Smart Nation initiatives?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government be more selective in granting access to Singpass to more companies and services?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is something which Member Mr Murali raised earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, what measures are in place to mitigate the risks associated with the exposure of Singpass credentials, if these services are compromised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can the security of users' credentials be guaranteed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure the full support of our people in our Smart Nation ambition, we must build their confidence not only in the robustness of our cyber networks and systems, but also in the solutions available, in case of system failures and vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Citizens should not have to fear losing money or personal data with each attempt to conduct a digital transaction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, some aspects of the Bills pose concern for seniors, who may be less savvy with online transactions and scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many banks are shifting towards digital transactions, which is disconcerting for seniors who may not be familiar with online banking technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite the lack of confidence, some of them invariably may have to resort to conducting their banking activities online.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such cases, they may seek assistance from others, which puts them at risk, if these individuals have malicious intentions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the law address cases where seniors willingly hand over control of their Singpass or bank accounts to family members or caregivers who may then use them for illegal activities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures will be taken to mitigate the exploitation of seniors who may not fully understand the nature of their actions, when transferring money under the guidance of others, such as "friends" or acquaintances?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my Yio Chu Kang estate, there are many senior residents who live alone or spend a significant amount of time alone as their children are working.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These vulnerable individuals are often not digitally savvy, making them more susceptible to falling prey to scammers who pose as friends or manipulate or force them into becoming money mules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Scammers often take advantage of their victims' fears and insecurities to extract more money or account information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the victims' accounts are frozen due to illegal activity, they face a double whammy of being charged with a criminal offence for acting out of fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While my grassroots leaders and I do our best to raise awareness, emotions and panic tend to cloud judgement, as often seen in love or kidnap scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the law consider the circumstances and susceptibility of elderly victims in these cases?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another important consideration is how the proposed law will affect our ongoing efforts to educate seniors about digital and cyber safety, such as the Seniors Go Digital initiative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the law make seniors more apprehensive about using digital technology and undermine our progress in this area?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is disheartening to hear seniors express reluctance to transact online when we discuss new scams with them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their reaction suggests that they may forsake digital transactions altogether, to avoid the risk of being scammed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But there needs to be a balance between allowing for easier prosecution and collaborators who may have genuinely been misled by syndicates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot ignore the fact that vulnerable seniors and genuine scam victims exist.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must adopt a comprehensive approach to safeguard our seniors' personal data, whilst also provide education on digital and cyber safety to vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The number of reported scams and the amount lost to scams are steadily increasing, with significant impact on individuals and their hard-earned money.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) at Pasir Ris, one of my residents, who is a professional, came up to me, sharing that he had lost more than $200,000 to a scam and that the majority of the money lost was his mother's retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is essential to address this issue promptly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whilst scammers continue to change their modus operandi, our agencies are diligently working to catch up with them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is encouraging to witness the collaboration between the MHA and the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office as they work closely together to strengthen our collective defence against scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I have three points of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My first point will be on clarifying some of the clauses in the amendments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My second point will focus on how we continue to educate the general public effectively on scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And my third and last point will be focusing on how we improve the recovery of the monies lost to scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The proposed amendments in the Bills stipulate that the payment account owners, including bank accounts, must exercise responsible conduct in the utilisation of the said account.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They will be held accountable for any transaction that takes place through their accounts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In considering requests by others to use their payment accounts to receive and transfer monies, owners are always expected to find out more about the other party, to verify the other party's identity and to understand the origin or destination of the monies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can I confirm with the Second Minister that payment accounts include other types of platforms beyond banks or Singpass accounts, such as e-wallets like Apple Pay, Samsung Pay, Grab Pay, Google Pay and We Chat Pay?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the amendments, when an account owner receives money from or transfers money to another person, he must also take reasonable steps to enquire and identify the source or destination of the money.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He would be deemed to have acted rashly if he proceeded to carry out transactions while he had suspicions, but did not make further enquiries to address those suspicions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, he would be deemed to have acted negligently if he continues with a transaction despite the presence of "red flags" that are noticeable by an ordinary, responsible person.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that scammers will often impersonate officials, trusted entities and even family members, what is the threshold required to prove that the account owner has acted negligently or recklessly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Very often we hear of how victims were completely convinced that the scammers were from trusted sources.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The burden of proof has shifted and we must be careful how we manage this threshold, so as not to make it even more challenging for victims who have already lost their money and compound their predicament by holding them responsible for allowing money to be transacted out of their account.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The proposed amendments to the CMA were prompted by instances of Singpass account being sold by individuals, which is a worrisome occurrence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In light of this development, it is pertinent to inquire as to the current prevalence of such incidents and the total number of such cases reported to the Police.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For a second or subsequent offence, the maximum penalty will be a fine of up to $20,000 or imprisonment of up to five years, or both.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This seems similar to the penalty for theft.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, given that in Singapore, an individual's Singpass account provides access to many other facilities and has bigger implications if abused as compared to physical theft, the proposed penalties for obtaining or dealing with Singpass credentials should serve as an adequate deterrent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that this is enough of a deterrent to prevent the illegal sale and theft of Singpass account access?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This brings me to my second point of whether individuals who had sold or inadvertently divulged their Singpass details to scammers were cognisant of the potential ramifications of such actions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we continue to educate people on the importance of keeping this information private and not sharing it with others?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we continue to better educate people in ensuring that they always remain curious and enquire about sources and the destination of transactions and not just trust others openly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Educating the public about scams is crucial for prevention.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is a misconception that only the old and the digitally illiterate gets scammed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These individuals are digital natives, indicating a need for targeted education efforts that debunk misconceptions about scam victims and cater to the unique challenges faced by the younger generations too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we stop money from quickly exiting the accounts of the victims to multiple banks and then quickly channelled outside of our jurisdiction?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we balance between the efficiency of money transfers through banks versus providing adequate protection for victims of scams?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there a fail-safe system to immediately stop fraudulent transactions from crossing our boundaries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How much responsibility is placed on the banks to ensure that it is not easy for the scammers or money launderers to move money quickly around?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we using technology tools such as blockchain and AI to detect and prevent such fraudulent transactions?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To elaborate more on my last point, the continuous rise in the number of scam cases is deeply concerning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, the number of scam cases reported in 2022 at 31,728 cases is far higher, almost 50% more than the number of cases of physical crimes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our hon colleague Mr Murali earlier mentioned, the number of scam cases has reached an industrial scale.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we have enough resources and capability along with the correct organisational structure within our Police force to take on this changing nature of crimes effectively?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can our Police force be equipped with the right technology like generative AI to help "patrol" the digital space and investigate such crimes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   The rise in scam cases continues to be a worrying trend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The number of cases and amount lost to scams continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The modus operandi of scammers changes frequently, and our agencies are working together to strengthen our collective defence against scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I have three points of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The first point seeks clarification on some clauses in the amendments, namely, to ensure that this Bill covers all forms of payment, not just bank accounts, but also e-wallets, such as Google Pay or Apple Pay.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, while the amendments mean that account holders will be responsible if there are fraudulent transactions going through their account, we must ensure that we set the threshold so that we do not make it even harder for scam victims who have already lost their money.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, we must continue to stay vigilant and further enhance our capabilities to work together to prevent and stop these scams.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I am pleased to see how our agencies are working together to strengthen our collective defence against scams with the amendments to the Bills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I stand in support the Bills.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most worryingly, more Singaporeans are falling prey to such scams, and national statistics aside, on a local level, I have seen a stark increase of residents coming to see me at MPS on scam matters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some devastated, seeking justice for monies and life savings lost, some seething, seeking redress for loved ones who have been found guilty of being involved in scams.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Dealing with scams presents a set of distinct and novel challenges for law enforcement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To navigate and patrol the digital space while ensuring freedoms and privacy of our citizens will be a perennial balancing act; to heavily monitor and limit online interaction presents not only an ethical conundrum of over-policing, but also an operational problem, given the rapidly changing techniques and technology that is used by scammers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I support the intention and aim of these amendments, I cannot help but consider the potential repercussions of placing significant onus on individuals to take responsibility for how they dispense and share their personal data online, especially in the ever-evolving situation of scams.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In an age where there is an ever-growing digitalisation of i-banking and Government services that require the use of bank accounts and Singpass details, we have to be mindful of how this Bill may implicate those in our society who are not tech-natives, particularly our senior citizens, and persons with special needs and mental disabilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Scams today are no longer overt, blatant advertisements which are easily recognisable, but they reach us in a host of ways that can appear subtle and very genuine.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just last evening, after MPS, one of my volunteers, a smart savvy individual in his 40s, sheepishly admitted to me that he was a phishing scam victim last year, having inadvertently given his OTP to a fake delivery site.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, by transferring the responsibility of online vigilance onto our senior citizens, or our less digitally inclined, it presents a twofold problem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For such seniors, they not only suffer financial loss as victims of scams, but are re-victimised by their "failed" attempt to utilise digital services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, by shifting the onus onto the individual, I fear the impact it may have on vulnerable communities such as adults with special needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If one struggles with managing sensitive data on a day-to-day basis, doing so in the complex digital sphere without empathetic safeguards can only be exponentially more difficult.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A conversation with a resident in my constituency highlighted the struggles her stepson faces as an adult with special needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without the right to create a bank account, the family faced much difficulty in receiving monies due to him via his father's will when his father passed on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the world become ever more dependent on digital services for daily functions, we must continue to consider what byproducts our laws may have on those on the fringes of society and ensure that we do not systematically inhibit the access to the life they desire.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the spirit of "Forward Singapore", I believe that this Bill is best served with supplementary safeguards and policies to ensure our vulnerable communities are not inadvertently affected.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to provide and amplify present digital literacy initiatives for seniors and other vulnerable members of our community who face difficulty dealing with the growing digitalisation of Government and banking services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, given the ever-evolving nature of scams, we need to keep on our toes and feed our communities through digital ambassadors and other agency representatives active in our local community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I call on the Ministry, as we enhance our crime enforcement safety nets, to also augment this with community outreach efforts to provide timely and up-to-date scam advisories, enabling our communities to develop long-term know-how on identifying and reacting to scams.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, the Government should not be the sole stakeholder to ameliorate potential gaps.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Banks and other digital platforms can do more to provide additional protection for our vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Creating sandboxes to experiment with new solutions, such as increased levels of authentication or the tailoring of experiences suitable to certain age groups or demographics, may be the first step towards mitigating the exposure to scams and providing financial inclusion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we address the present lapses in our efforts to combat scams, I hope that we do not lose sight of the potential effects this new Bill can have on our technologically vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to be cognisant of the implications in placing greater responsibility on individuals to navigate the digital world, seek to provide support and aid and ensure that we do not leave vulnerable groups to greater risk and alienation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The eight Members who spoke raised important questions, which I will try my best to address.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They raised two broad types of concerns: one, what if a person was genuinely tricked into giving up control of their bank accounts or disclosing their Singpass credentials; and two, what if a person needed help making transactions and gave up control of their bank accounts or disclosed their Singpass credentials to a family member or friend, and subsequently had their trust betrayed?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Yip shared his strong belief that our public prosecutors and Police Officers will act judiciously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police also recognise that there are indeed situations where there is a genuine need to share credentials for legitimate transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police will investigate the cases comprehensively, considering factors such as the person's mental capacity – which Ms Lim, Ms Yeo and Mr Ng all asked about – and also the context of the incident.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will consider any credible evidence that a person was genuinely tricked into entering their banking or Singpass credentials on phishing websites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The AGC will also carefully consider each case on its own facts and circumstances, and assess if there is public interest to pursue prosecution even if the evidential threshold is crossed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain cited a story of a 19-year-old who responded to a job ad and gave up control of his bank and Singpass account to an unknown employer he had never met, for income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
